title: Salvation
lead: To "save" in the Bible is to rescue: from enemies, from exile, from sickness, from sin and death. The Old Testament speaks of the LORD saving Israel at the sea and in later crises; the New Testament says that God saves through Jesus, from the coming judgment, and gives new life now. Churches differ on how salvation is received, whether it can be lost, and who can be saved.

sections.b: The Exodus is the pattern: the LORD saved Israel from Egypt at the sea (Exodus 14:30). The Psalms cry to God to save, and Isaiah promises a coming salvation for Israel and the nations.

The name Jesus means "the LORD saves." Peter says there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). In Romans salvation is mostly future, rescue from the coming anger, but already begun by justification. The New Testament has three tenses: we were saved, are being saved and will be saved.
sections.refs: Matthew 1:21; Acts 4:12; Romans 1:16; Romans 5:9–10; Romans 10:9–13; Ephesians 2:8–10; 1 Peter 1:5
